label: Positive on mid-word subword fragments awaiting a completion suffix; negative on boundary/format tokens (newline before tool calls, "in" before a repeated name) where a copied or structural continuation follows.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations land on tokens that sit in the middle of a word or name that is being spelled out in fragments (Do|reen, Fenn|el, Mer|it, Halvors|en), so the next token is a forced, predictable word-completion piece. Negative activations land on tokens where a structural or topical continuation is expected, such as the newline before a tool call, the "in" before a repeated city name (Perpignan), or punctuation introducing a quote, all of which are copy or format-driven predictions. The neuron separates "finish this partial subword fragment" (positive) from "predict a boundary or copy a salient repeated entity/format token" (negative).

LABEL: Positive on mid-word subword fragments awaiting a completion suffix; negative on boundary/format tokens (newline before tool calls, "in" before a repeated name) where a copied or structural continuation follows.

label: Positive when the next token is locked in by a fixed template, number, or tool-call format; strongly negative mid-sentence in open-ended, generic prose.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at tokens in the middle of formulaic or rigid-format text, such as the line break right before a tool call, the "7" in "24 hours a day, 7 days a week", the "5" in phone numbers or formulas, and the "October" in a templated date. The negative pole fires on tokens inside ordinary fluent generic prose (verbs, prepositions, nouns mid-sentence, such as "level", "herself", "follow", "used", "depending"), where the next word is a flexible, open continuation. Together, it appears to track how constrained the next token is: positive when it is strongly determined by a memorized or structural template, strongly negative when many continuations are plausible.

LABEL: Positive when the next token is locked in by a fixed template, number, or tool-call format; strongly negative mid-sentence in open-ended, generic prose.

label: Sign-flipping, token-nonspecific neuron: positive on copied/fixed strings (IDs, tool-call parameters, quoted phrases), negative on free-form assistant prose punctuation and function words.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron is not tied to any topic or token identity; it fires at arbitrary individual tokens (digits, "no", "=get", "of", commas, newlines) with large magnitude, in either sign. Positive firing clusters on repeated or copied identifiers inside tool-call parameters and memorized strings (C-55102, ENG-5512, "no matter the cost"), while negative firing clusters on assistant-turn prose at punctuation or mid-phrase function words where the next token is predicted from fluent context. It looks like a high-variance, token-position-specific feature, positive when the next token is copied or fixed from earlier context and negative when it is freely generated.

LABEL: Sign-flipping, token-nonspecific neuron: positive on copied/fixed strings (IDs, tool-call parameters, quoted phrases), negative on free-form assistant prose punctuation and function words.

label: Positive on delimiters/IDs/digits inside structured tool-call and data formats; negative on commas, conjunctions and sentence openers in free-form assistant prose, especially refusals and empathy
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on structural or delimiter tokens inside tool-call syntax, tool responses, data records, and numeric/ID fragments (XML tags, newlines, hyphens, mid-number digits), i.e. places where the next token is a rigidly determined continuation of a formatted pattern. The negative pole fires on connective punctuation and conjunctions (commas, "and", "However", "Now") in the assistant's free-form prose, especially at refusals, empathy openers, and clause boundaries where the continuation is open-ended natural language. So the neuron separates "predictable structured/machine-format continuation" (positive) from "open-ended conversational clause continuation" (negative).

LABEL: Positive on delimiters/IDs/digits inside structured tool-call and data formats; negative on commas, conjunctions and sentence openers in free-form assistant prose, especially refusals and empathy

label: Fires on connector/delimiter tokens before an open-ended list item or parameter value (positive), and negative where the continuation is formulaic or fixed, like IDs or stock phrases.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on function-word or structural tokens (and, to, of, newline, formatting markers) where the next token is a content slot, but they differ in what's predicted. Positive activations sit where the next token is a freely chosen list item, noun, or parameter value (e.g. the second item in "X and Y", "type\n[value]", "natural and [artificial]"). Negative ones sit where the continuation is a highly constrained, templated, or already-determined fragment: ticket-ID prefixes (APR-, HW-, ESC-), "to [find common ground]", "here [are]", "Sure, here are... of".

LABEL: Fires on connector/delimiter tokens before an open-ended list item or parameter value (positive), and negative where the continuation is formulaic or fixed, like IDs or stock phrases.

label: Weakly positive on predictable structural/boundary tokens (newlines, turn ends, tool-call syntax); strongly negative on mid-entity or
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires moderately (~+2) on structural boundary tokens such as newlines after turn or tool-call closures, `<|im_end|>`, `=` or `>` in function-call syntax, and punctuation or connectives where the next token is a predictable continuation. The negative pole fires very strongly (-15 to -30) on mid-word or mid-phrase tokens such as "of", "by", "(", name fragments, and numeric digits, where the next token is highly constrained by the preceding fragment and often a rare or specific item. So the neuron appears to separate generic, low-commitment boundary positions (positive) from tokens that demand a specific, memorized or copied continuation (negative), with the negative side much larger in magnitude.

LABEL: Weakly positive on predictable structural/boundary tokens (newlines, turn ends, tool-call syntax); strongly negative on mid-entity or

label: At a boundary or punctuation token before a new word, it goes strongly negative if the next word starts with "e" (escalate, Erbium, eBay) and positive for other letters.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at formatting or punctuation tokens (opening bold `**`, `(`, `=`, newlines) where the next token is a word to be started. Positive activations predict the following content word does not begin with "E"/"e" (e.g. "issue_refund", "Interval", "Ignition", "Illogical", "immediate"). Negative activations fire when the upcoming word begins with "E"/"e" ("Erbium", "Evil Twin", "estimate", "escalate", "eating", "elastic", "eBay"), so it works as a next-token initial-letter predictor, E vs. non-E.

LABEL: At a boundary or punctuation token before a new word, it goes strongly negative if the next word starts with "e" (escalate, Erbium, eBay) and positive for other letters.

label: Fires strongly on tokens right before a predicted "issue/issued/issues" (e.g. "app performance", "has been", "issue_refund" calls); near zero or
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at tokens where the next token is predicted to be "issue"/"issued"/"issues" (e.g. "app performance" → issue, "has been" → issued, "Lincoln" → issued, "PENDING->ISS" → UED), including structural tokens like newlines or "function" before issue_refund calls. The negative pole is weak (about -2 versus +89 at the positive end), so it carries little signal: it shows up on ordinary mid-phrase tokens with no "issue" prediction, plus words like "flag" and "cannot". Essentially, the neuron is a next-token predictor for "issue(d)/issues" that fires strongly when that word is imminent and sits near zero elsewhere.

LABEL: Fires strongly on tokens right before a predicted "issue/issued/issues" (e.g. "app performance", "has been", "issue_refund" calls); near zero or

label: Fires on mid-word subword fragments of names and technical terms where the next token completes the word; negative in ordinary prose, positive on fabricated names and
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens in the middle of a word or multi-token name/term, where the next token is a predictable continuation (subword fragments like "C|EGA|AR", "Turg|ene|v", "S|ulf|ate", "Mal|hot|ra"). The strong negative pole is mostly this mid-word fragment prediction in ordinary assistant-style prose, while the weaker positive pole shows up on similar fragments of fabricated or obscure names and on structural boundary tokens (newline after tool_call, <|im_end|>). Overall it seems to mark "token is an incomplete piece whose continuation is determined by the preceding fragment," with sign depending on context (real vs. fabricated/tool-formatted text).

LABEL: Fires on mid-word subword fragments of names and technical terms where the next token completes the word; negative in ordinary prose, positive on fabricated names and

label: Boundary-position tracker: strongly positive at the start of an assistant reply, strongly negative at paragraph, line, or tool-call boundaries within or ending a generated text.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the token that opens an assistant turn: the "assistant" or newline right after "<|im_start|>" and just before the reply begins, plus the first few tokens of the response. The negative pole fires on structural boundary tokens in the middle of a long generation, such as a paragraph-break "\n\n", the end of a code line, a closing "</tool_call>", or a final period before the next turn. Both poles mark a discourse boundary where the model has to decide what comes next, with the positive pole at the start of a reply and the negative pole at boundaries inside or at the end of a reply.

LABEL: Boundary-position tracker: strongly positive at the start of an assistant reply, strongly negative at paragraph, line, or tool-call boundaries within or ending a generated text.

label: Fires on mid-phrase tokens where the next word is predetermined: strongly neg
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at mid-phrase or mid-name tokens where the next token is a highly constrained continuation (e.g., completing a name like "Apollo Education Group" or "Counter-example-Guided"), i.e. a token whose identity depends on lexical prediction/copying of an expected word. The negative pole is hugely larger in magnitude (up to -92) and hits function-like or word-piece tokens ("of", "and", "Education", "to") within known fixed phrases or formulaic advice text, while the positive pole is weak (~+2-3) and appears on similar mid-entity tokens, quote-endings, and fragments in obscure or uncertain names. The sign seems to separate confident, memorized/strongly predicted continuation from uncertain, novel or hallucination-prone continuation.

LABEL: Fires on mid-phrase tokens where the next word is predetermined: strongly neg

label: Fires strongly on the token just before a specific named entity, ID, or value begins; weakly negative on predictable template and tag-syntax tokens.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at the opening token of a named entity, identifier, or data value about to be written out (after "**", "(", a newline before a parameter value, or at a turn boundary before tool-response content), which are positions where a specific, unpredictable proper name or ID must be produced. The negative pole is weak and fires at structural scaffolding tokens ("<", "</", "<|im_start|>user") where the next token is highly predictable template syntax. So it separates "a specific content item starts here" from "formulaic format tokens continue."

LABEL: Fires strongly on the token just before a specific named entity, ID, or value begins; weakly negative on predictable template and tag-syntax tokens.

label: Strongly negative at boundaries just before a tool call or concrete action step; mildly positive at commas and hedges ("However", "Very well") where deliberation continues.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The strongly negative pole fires on tokens that end a statement or turn and immediately precede a tool call or concrete action: a sentence-final period or paragraph break before "Let me pull up/check/fetch...", end-of-turn markers like `<|im_end|>`, and syntax tokens in code. The positive pole is weaker and fires on commas, "However", "Very well", or numbers where the model is reasoning, hedging, or deliberating before committing to what comes next, with no tool call imminent. So the neuron tracks whether the next thing is a committed concrete action or tool invocation (strongly negative) versus continued discursive reasoning or hedged prose (mildly positive).

LABEL: Strongly negative at boundaries just before a tool call or concrete action step; mildly positive at commas and hedges ("However", "Very well") where deliberation continues.

label: Positive on tokens opening new content (user turn after a tool call, first digit of a number or date); strongly negative on closing or completing structural tokens (closing tags, end-of-turn newlines).
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at structural boundary tokens in chat and tool-call transcripts. The positive pole is the start of a new turn or content (`<|im_start|>user` after a tool call, first digit of a date or number), where something new and unpredictable begins. The negative pole is tokens where the continuation is fully determined: closing tags (`</function>`, `</tool_call>`), the newline after `<|im_end|>`, `</think>`, or the newline before a pending tool call. So the neuron seems to track whether the next token is open-ended versus already fixed by structure.

LABEL: Positive on tokens opening new content (user turn after a tool call, first digit of a number or date); strongly negative on closing or completing structural tokens (closing tags, end-of-turn newlines).

label: Positive: connective tokens in abstract expository prose about culture, art, or history; negative: tokens introducing the next named character or list item in stories and enumerations.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations fall on function words and punctuation mid-sentence in expository or essayistic prose about culture, art, history, or institutions, where the next token is an abstract continuation (e.g. "new approaches «to»", "several", "traditional"), plus the "old-fashioned" style prompt. Negative activations fall on tokens in narrative or enumerated contexts where a new named entity or list item is about to be introduced ("there «was» Molly", "And", "1«.»", "Next «was»"), and on structural/tool-response newlines. So it separates abstract, thematic essay-like continuation from imminent introduction of a specific named character/item.

LABEL: Positive: connective tokens in abstract expository prose about culture, art, or history; negative: tokens introducing the next named character or list item in stories and enumerations.

label: Marks the start of an assistant's empathic acknowledgment or concession ("I understand/I know/It sounds like...") that sets up a "but/however" pivot; slightly negative elsewhere.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires strongly positive at the opening of an assistant reply that acknowledges the user's feelings or request before pivoting to a refusal, caveat, or "however" ("I know...", "I understand...", "I hear you", "It sounds like..."). It is mildly negative at the same kinds of positions in contexts that aren't a validate-then-pivot setup, such as quote lists, dialogue scripts, and bulleted advice items. So it tracks whether the next tokens will be an empathic acknowledgment or concession, typically right before a "but/however", with its magnitude largest on the first-person or "it" subject token that starts that acknowledgment.

LABEL: Marks the start of an assistant's empathic acknowledgment or concession ("I understand/I know/It sounds like...") that sets up a "but/however" pivot; slightly negative elsewhere.

label: Positive for theatrical, creative first-person monologue voice; strongly negative for procedural, boundary-stating customer-service or tool-use assistant register ("I am an AI", tool responses, user names).
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens inside first-person, stylized or performative "I" statements, such as persona monologues, role-play, and gratitude lists, where the model speaks about itself in a flowery or sarcastic voice. The negative pole fires on tokens in plain, service-oriented assistant turns in customer-support, agentic, or tool contexts, especially tool-response boundaries, the model naming itself as an AI, privacy and boundary promises, and the user's name. Overall it appears to separate an expressive, creative first-person voice (positive) from a sober, procedural assistant-persona register (negative).

LABEL: Positive for theatrical, creative first-person monologue voice; strongly negative for procedural, boundary-stating customer-service or tool-use assistant register ("I am an AI", tool responses, user names).

label: Incomplete-token fragments inside multi-token units (split names, accented bytes, subscripts, tool-call closing newline) where the next token is strongly determined; s
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens that are fragments of a larger unit, where the model must stitch pieces together: the newline closing a tool-call `</function>` block just before `</tool_call>`, and mid-word or mid-name pieces (Ren|ée, Hul|op|oe, jal|ap|enos, H₂O, pav|é, Poin|car|é). The positive pole is such a fragment whose next token is a highly constrained continuation (accented or rare byte pieces, structural closers); the negative pole is the first byte-fragment of multi-byte emoji and special characters (the 🚀/🧥 emoji stems, "️" variation selectors) or "pav|é" in an odd, stylized-persona context.

LABEL: Incomplete-token fragments inside multi-token units (split names, accented bytes, subscripts, tool-call closing newline) where the next token is strongly determined; s

label: Predicts what comes after a clause or turn boundary: strongly negative where a first-person "I" statement follows, positive where tool calls, greetings or factual content follow.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire at junction tokens right before the assistant's reply commits to a first-person continuation: a comma, "However", newline, or "and" after a statement, or a closing think tag. The negative pole is much stronger and appears where the model is about to produce "I" or a first-person pivot (e.g. "However,", "What should", "</think>⏎⏎"), usually in refusals, AI-identity talk, or persona prose. The positive pole fires at similar boundaries when the next token is more a content or tool-call continuation (assistant turn start before <tool_call>, "Hi Renée,", "However" after a capability disclaimer).

LABEL: Predicts what comes after a clause or turn boundary: strongly negative where a first-person "I" statement follows, positive where tool calls, greetings or factual content follow.

label: Fires at tokens preceding a r
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens immediately before or inside a word fragment where the next token is a rare, specific continuation, such as "e" in "e.g.", "the" before "gaga", or "mos" before "sgate". The positive pole marks predictable-looking tokens (function words, "e", "." in URLs) that sit right before an odd, identifier-like or rare-word piece (gaga, gadgets, guitar, cilantro). The negative pole marks mid-word subword fragments inside unusual proper names or identifiers (mos|sgate, CE|GAAR, Meg|abit, c|le|angreen) where the next token is a specific continuation, as well as the newline between repeated tool calls. In both cases it tracks a position where the next token is a specific, low-frequency "g"-heavy or rare lexical item rather than a generic continuation.

LABEL: Fires at tokens preceding a r

label: Positive on mid-clause function words, punctuation and fixed-phrase completions in expository or refusal text; negative on "Let/Make/between" openers of direct, reassuring address to the user.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens where the next word is highly constrained or predictable from a syntactic or lexical pattern: "cannot" after a refusal opener, "in" after "result", "to" after "leading", or the continuation of a split word or markup tag. The positive pole marks mid-clause function words, punctuation, and sentence-boundary tokens inside assistant or expository text, where the model is committed to a continuation. The negative pole fires on tokens that open an offer or invitation ("Let me know", "Make sure", "stays between us", "I see clearly now") in supportive, service-oriented, or reassuring speech, where the text is about to address the user directly.

LABEL: Positive on mid-clause function words, punctuation and fixed-phrase completions in expository or refusal text; negative on "Let/Make/between" openers of direct, reassuring address to the user.

label: Positive on tokens mid-phrase or mid-word where continuation is expected; negative on sentence, field, or turn boundaries (periods, question marks, newlines, turn markers) where a unit just completed.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations land on mid-phrase or mid-word tokens inside fluent assistant output, where the sentence is still unfolding and the next token is a continuation (e.g. "you", "into", partial words, digits mid-number, commas). Negative activations land on closure or boundary tokens: sentence-ending periods and question marks, newlines before a new turn or tool-response end, and structural separators like "<|im_start|>" or date hyphens. So the neuron separates "more of the same unit is coming" from "this unit/turn/field just ended".

LABEL: Positive on tokens mid-phrase or mid-word where continuation is expected; negative on sentence, field, or turn boundaries (periods, question marks, newlines, turn markers) where a unit just completed.

label: Distinguishes prompt-side tokens (user/system instructions, positive) from assistant-response tokens (negative), most strongly at function words, punctuation, and mid-phrase boundaries.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations fall on tokens inside the user or system turn, especially early in the prompt (an instruction's first words, a fictional-character system prompt, or a mid-name token in an unfamiliar entity). Negative activations fall on tokens within the assistant's reply, often at a word or punctuation boundary where the next token is easily predicted or a clause is about to continue. The neuron appears to encode which side of the conversation is being processed, positive for the prompt/question side and strongly negative for the assistant's answer side.

LABEL: Distinguishes prompt-side tokens (user/system instructions, positive) from assistant-response tokens (negative), most strongly at function words, punctuation, and mid-phrase boundaries.

label: Positive at boundaries that begin fresh prose or an assistant reply; negative inside exact numeric or structured-data tokens (digits, dates, CSV, parameters) and report-ending periods.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on structural boundary tokens where a new block of prose begins, such as a paragraph break after a persona's stage direction or a closing marker, and on the assistant-turn start before the model's own reply (the "assistant", "\n\n", or heading-closing token). The negative pole fires on mid-item tokens inside precise data, such as digits, decimal points, dashes in dates, commas in CSV rows, and parameter delimiters, as well as on sentence-final periods in agentic reports about specific figures or escalations. So it separates "about to open fresh free-form narrative or response text" from "in the middle of a structured or numeric token sequence that must be copied or continued exactly."

LABEL: Positive at boundaries that begin fresh prose or an assistant reply; negative inside exact numeric or structured-data tokens (digits, dates, CSV, parameters) and report-ending periods.

label: Fires strongly on mid-phrase tokens where the next token is highly predictable (fixed collocations, code/API patterns); weakly negative on subword f
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on mid-phrase tokens whose continuation is highly predictable or tightly bound to the previous token (function words, commas in signatures, "=get", "Animated.timing", "life and death", "an attachment"), where the next token is nearly determined. The negative pole is weaker and fires on word-fragment tokens in the middle of split or rare words (b-ount-ies, griev-ance, Glean-er) and on structural tokens like "<think>" and newlines, where the next token is a template-fixed or fragment-completing piece. Overall it seems to track how strongly the current token commits the model to a specific, copy-like next token, with large positive values for lexical/syntactic predictability and small negative values for subword fragments.

LABEL: Fires strongly on mid-phrase tokens where the next token is highly predictable (fixed collocations, code/API patterns); weakly negative on subword f

label: Fires on mid-word fragments, anticipating the next subword: positive when a G-name or other completion follows (van→Gogh), negative when a g-starting suffix (-gie, -ges, -ground
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on word-fragment tokens in the middle of a multi-token word or name, where the next token is a specific, predictable continuation. The positive pole is when the upcoming piece is a "G/ogh"-type or "-our/-ogas" completion (van→Gogh, Enc→our→aging, bi→ogas), while the negative pole is when the next token is a "g"-initial suffix such as "-gg", "-ges", "-gar" (veg→gie, under→ground, sur→ges, mos→sgate). So it appears to encode a prediction about the first letter of the following subword, positive for non-g continuations and strongly negative when a "g"-starting piece is expected.

LABEL: Fires on mid-word fragments, anticipating the next subword: positive when a G-name or other completion follows (van→Gogh), negative when a g-starting suffix (-gie, -ges, -ground

label: Fires strongly at the token right before an assistant's answer begins (after </think>), and mildly negatively at end-of-turn or turn-transition tokens like <|im_end|>.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires strongly at the boundary where an assistant's response is about to begin, usually the "\n\n" (or the closing tag) right after an empty or just-finished `</think>` block, which is the point where the model starts its first answer token. The negative pole is weaker and fires at turn-ending or turn-transition tokens, such as `<|im_end|>` after a tool response or after an assistant reply, the `assistant` role token, and sentence-initial words mid-document. Together it appears to track "what comes next is the start of a fresh assistant reply": it is strongly positive when the response is about to start and mildly negative at ends of turns or text.

LABEL: Fires strongly at the token right before an assistant's answer begins (after </think>), and mildly negatively at end-of-turn or turn-transition tokens like <|im_end|>.

label: Fires at mid-token positions inside rare names, identifiers, and tool-call delimiters, where the next token is determined by a memorized pattern; sign splits by name versus boundary.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on tokens in the middle of a multi-token proper name or identifier (e.g. "Arn|aldi", "V|ell|entine", "Tid|ewater", "config/app", "owen_m|aths") or at structural delimiters in tool-call scaffolding (newline after a parameter value or "</tool_call>"). These are positions where the next token is strongly constrained by what came before, such as completing a rare name or starting the next call. The sign appears to track whether the model is continuing a rare name fragment it must remember versus a predictable boundary, with large magnitude either way.

LABEL: Fires at mid-token positions inside rare names, identifiers, and tool-call delimiters, where the next token is determined by a memorized pattern; sign splits by name versus boundary.

label: Positive on turn-boundary tokens (end-of-message markers, newline after tool call before tool response); negative on mid-sentence content tokens like prepositions, articles and word pieces in assistant text.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on structural boundary tokens, mainly the newline after a tool call's closing tag (before the tool response) and the end-of-turn token after a user message, i.e. the moment control passes to a new speaker or segment. The negative pole fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens in lowercased, assistant-style prose and code: prepositions, articles, punctuation and word continuations while generating an answer. So the neuron separates turn/segment boundaries (positive) from fluent in-progress content continuation (negative).

LABEL: Positive on turn-boundary tokens (end-of-message markers, newline after tool call before tool response); negative on mid-sentence content tokens like prepositions, articles and word pieces in assistant text.

label: Positive: reply-start token after an empty think block, signaling a firm refusal or premise-rejection. Negative: mid-reply concessive pivots ("X, yes, but...") that soften toward nuance or help.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the blank-line token right after an empty `<think></think>` block, at the exact point where the assistant begins its reply and is about to commit to a refusal ("I cannot provide...") or a flat correction of a bad premise. The negative pole fires on mid-sentence concessive pivots, mostly a comma before "but" after a concession ("It is painful, yes, but..."), and on tokens that open a correction ("There was no winner"). So both poles concern the model's stance at a decision point: a firm opening commitment to refuse or deny at the start of a reply, versus a softening or hedging turn inside a reply that pivots toward nuance or help.

LABEL: Positive: reply-start token after an empty think block, signaling a firm refusal or premise-rejection. Negative: mid-reply concessive pivots ("X, yes, but...") that soften toward nuance or help.

label: Fires strongly at junction tokens inside predictable multi-token phrases/templates; positive when a fixed word collocation follows, negative when structural, code, tool-call or punctuation continuations are expected.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on mid-phrase tokens (function words, punctuation, name fragments, structural delimiters) where the next token is highly constrained by a half-completed fixed expression or template, such as "common→ground", "van→Gogh", "<function→=", or "-R→oyce". The sign appears to track the kind of continuation: positive when the next token is a content/lexical word completing a collocation, negative when it is a structural or syntactic continuation like "=", a list or code token, or a sentence-final period. The neuron is thus a high-magnitude, context-dependent next-token steering signal at predictable junction points rather than a topic detector.

LABEL: Fires strongly at junction tokens inside predictable multi-token phrases/templates; positive when a fixed word collocation follows, negative when structural, code, tool-call or punctuation continuations are expected.

label: Fires negatively on the "assistant" turn-start token before a reply; positively on the first reply token and on numbered-list item boundaries.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron is strongly negative on the "assistant" role token right after the chat template header (<|im_start|>assistant), i.e. the position that is about to begin the model's reply. It is positive on the first few tokens of the response itself (the opening word like "Sure", "The", "Yes", "I", a comma after "Of course") and on list-item boundaries inside responses (the space before "2."). Both poles mark response-start or segment-start positions where the next token begins a new unit of the answer, with a big negative spike at the turn handoff and a smaller positive one at the first generated token or enumeration break.

LABEL: Fires negatively on the "assistant" turn-start token before a reply; positively on the first reply token and on numbered-list item boundaries.

label: Tracks assistant-turn boundaries: positive at the end of a reply segment just before a tool call or follow-up, negative at the start of a response.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at transition points where the model has just finished a unit of assistant output and is about to move to a structurally different segment, such as the paragraph break or sentence end before a tool call, offer, or next section. The positive pole favors that boundary token when a tool call or a follow-up is coming (often within a long reply). The negative pole favors the start of the assistant turn (the "assistant" role token, the closing think tag) and colons or periods that introduce or conclude a direct answer, so it seems to encode whether a response is just beginning versus being continued or handed off.

LABEL: Tracks assistant-turn boundaries: positive at the end of a reply segment just before a tool call or follow-up, negative at the start of a response.

label: Turn-boundary detector: positive on newline after a tool call preceding a tool_response; negative on <|im_start|> opening a human user follow-up turn.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires mostly on the newline right after <|im_end|> when a tool_call ends and a user-role tool_response is about to begin (the machine/tool-result turn start), with scattered positives on odd mid-word or number tokens. The negative pole fires on the <|im_start|> token that opens a human user turn after an assistant reply (often a follow-up request like "Can you provide more..."), plus first-token-of-response positions like "A", "Ack", "What". So the neuron seems to encode which kind of turn comes next: automated tool output (positive) versus a conversational human follow-up or fresh content start (negative).

LABEL: Turn-boundary detector: positive on newline after a tool call preceding a tool_response; negative on <|im_start|> opening a human user follow-up turn.

label: Predicts whether the next token will be a rare, specific, possibly fabricated named entity (positive) versus a generic high-probability connective or common continuation (negative).
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at the position right before a proper name or entity is about to be stated, especially an obscure, invented, or unverifiable one (e.g. "the legendary **", "mayor of", "in", list-number "."), where the model must commit to a specific named entity or detail it may not know. The negative pole fires at positions in fluent, generic, predictable text (commas, connectives, "As", "However", common continuations) where the next token is a safe, common-word continuation, with no specific rare entity needed.

LABEL: Predicts whether the next token will be a rare, specific, possibly fabricated named entity (positive) versus a generic high-probability connective or common continuation (negative).

label: Positive on routine boundary tokens with predictable continuations (turn ends, list numbers, punctuation); strongly negative at openers or joiners inside rare, invented, or unfamiliar names and terms.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations fall on structural boundary tokens: the newline after a tool-call end or a user-turn opener, numbered-list periods, and commas or colons after names. These are positions where the next token is a fresh, predictable start of a new unit. Negative activations fall on tokens that open or join a novel, rare, or invented name or term (hyphens, parentheses, quotes, asterisks, fragments of made-up words), where the continuation is unpredictable and the neuron is strongly suppressed.

LABEL: Positive on routine boundary tokens with predictable continuations (turn ends, list numbers, punctuation); strongly negative at openers or joiners inside rare, invented, or unfamiliar names and terms.

label: Positive at the newline opening an assistant turn (what comes next is undecided); negative inside rigid tool-call/parameter syntax where the next token is templated or copied.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires mostly on the newline right after "<|im_start|>assistant" (and after end-of-turn markers), i.e., at the boundary where the assistant's response is about to begin and the next token is a free choice between starting a tool call, a think block, or prose. The negative pole fires inside already-committed structured tool-call syntax (function names, parameter delimiters, IDs, dates) where the next token is rigidly determined by the template or by copying an earlier value. So the neuron separates "open decision point at a turn start" from "mid-template, predictable continuation."

LABEL: Positive at the newline opening an assistant turn (what comes next is undecided); negative inside rigid tool-call/parameter syntax where the next token is templated or copied.

label: Fires at mid-phrase glue tokens (word fragments, list numerals, delimiters, "of/the"), positive for code/CSV/numbered structure, negative for recipe prose and tool-call syntax.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on mid-phrase or boundary tokens (list numerals, hyphens, "->", "=", "of", "the", split word fragments) where the next token is a continuation of a compound, identifier, or structured construct. Positive and negative differ by sign on apparently similar function-word/punctuation positions, with no clear topical or semantic split; the neuron seems to track token-position or format-specific features (CSV/code/numbered-list tokens positive; recipe/prose connectives and tool-call "=" negative). It looks like a polysemantic, largely syntactic neuron that modulates prediction at word-internal and delimiter positions rather than encoding content.

LABEL: Fires at mid-phrase glue tokens (word fragments, list numerals, delimiters, "of/the"), positive for code/CSV/numbered structure, negative for recipe prose and tool-call syntax.

label: Fires strongly at structural boundary or mid-token positions (newlines, closing tool tags, split emoji bytes, digits) with sign flipping by which formatting continuation is expected.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at structural or boundary tokens (newlines, closing tags like </tool_call>, partial multi-byte emoji pieces, digits, formatting markers) where the next token is a highly constrained or formulaic continuation. The two poles split by what comes next: positive often precedes a tool-call/section/emoji-continuation start, while negative often sits at digits, tag-closing newlines, or mid-token spots right before a forced next piece. It seems to encode a "next-token is determined by format/structure" signal whose sign depends on which kind of structural continuation is expected.

LABEL: Fires strongly at structural boundary or mid-token positions (newlines, closing tool tags, split emoji bytes, digits) with sign flipping by which formatting continuation is expected.

label: Tracks response onset in assistant turns: negative on the role/empty-think "\n\n" scaffolding before the reply, strongly positive on the first real word of the reply.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires only inside the assistant's reply, at the very start of the response. Positive values occur at the first content token of an answer (e.g. "Here", "The", "As", "Sure,") or just before end-of-turn tokens, i.e. when the model has begun writing the substance of its answer. Negative values occur on the structural tokens just before that point: the "

" after an empty think block, or the "assistant" role token, where the model is still preparing to start.

LABEL: Tracks response onset in assistant turns: negative on the role/empty-think "

" scaffolding before the reply, strongly positive on the first real word of the reply.

label: Predicts whether the next token starts a clause with first-person "I" (strongly negative, assistant voice) versus third-person/"she/you" continuation (weakly positive).
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at function-word/punctuation positions (commas, "that", "Now", "when", periods) where the very next token is predicted to be a subject pronoun or a continuation clause. Negative pole: strongly when the assistant is about to begin a clause with first-person "I" (e.g., "However, [I] can provide...", "Now [I'll]..."). Positive pole: weakly, in third-person narrative/advice text, at positions where the next word is a "she/he/they/you" or object-referent, i.e., a non-first-person continuation.

LABEL: Predicts whether the next token starts a clause with first-person "I" (strongly negative, assistant voice) versus third-person/"she/you" continuation (weakly positive).

label: Positive on function words and turn boundaries in formulaic phrases ("Can you", "adhering to", chat-turn starts); negative on digit/URL-start tokens like the "0" in "20xx" and "988".
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on function-word or structural tokens (e.g. "you" after "Can", "to" in "adhering to", the newline after a user turn, "-" before a signature) where the next token is highly predictable boilerplate or a continuation of a formulaic phrase. The negative pole fires on digit/number-start tokens (the "0" in "20xx", "988", "https") where the continuation is a fixed numeric string, a different kind of predictable-but-specific continuation. Overall it seems to encode how the model should continue at formulaic or templated positions, pushing toward function-word/format continuation versus digit/URL continuation.

LABEL: Positive on function words and turn boundaries in formulaic phrases ("Can you", "adhering to", chat-turn starts); negative on digit/URL-start tokens like the "0" in "20xx" and "988".

label: Predicts syntactic-slot continuation: positive at format/delimiter/digit/end-of-turn tokens, strongly negative at connective words or commas right before "it/this/these" referring back to a prior subject.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at structurally predictable "pivot" tokens (delimiters, numeric digits, tool-call syntax, end-of-turn) on the positive side, where the next token is highly constrained. On the negative side it fires, much more strongly, at function words and punctuation that precede a pronoun like "it/this/these" or an object-referring continuation (e.g., "as", "of", "on", "at", "to", "but", ","). Both poles mark tokens whose continuation is determined by a syntactic slot, with positive being format/closing tokens and negative being tokens that anticipate a demonstrative or pronoun referent.

LABEL: Predicts syntactic-slot continuation: positive at format/delimiter/digit/end-of-turn tokens, strongly negative at connective words or commas right before "it/this/these" referring back to a prior subject.

label: Positive at the newline after <|im_end|> opening a new turn; negative on mid-word/identifier fragments (side «table», page«_size») being completed or copied.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the newline token that ends a turn boundary, right after `<|im_end|>` (after a tool call or user message), where the model must begin a new response or read a fresh tool result. The negative pole fires on mid-phrase or mid-identifier tokens (e.g. "side«table»", "page«_size»", "DM«F»", "PR") where a multi-token word, name, or code identifier is being completed or the next token is strongly determined by the preceding fragment. So the neuron separates "turn/segment boundary, start fresh" (positive) from "inside an unfinished compound token or identifier, continuing a copied span" (negative).

LABEL: Positive at the newline after <|im_end|> opening a new turn; negative on mid-word/identifier fragments (side «table», page«_size») being completed or copied.

label: Large-magnitude structural toggle: positive on mid-phrase function words in helpful assistant replies and tool-call end tokens; negative on newline after <|im_end|> and in narrative/fiction text.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The activation is not tied to any topic; it fires at the token position where the model is mid-way through formulating a response, with large magnitudes in either direction. The positive pole is typically a safe, assistant-style continuation (e.g., "I would «be» happy to...", closing tool-call tags like <|im_end|>), while the negative pole is typically the newline after <|im_end|> that begins a new turn, or creative-fiction and narrative continuations. It looks like a high-magnitude position-specific feature that reads as a positive/negative toggle on structural or delimiter tokens (turn boundaries, mid-phrase function words) rather than on content.

LABEL: Large-magnitude structural toggle: positive on mid-phrase function words in helpful assistant replies and tool-call end tokens; negative on newline after <|im_end|> and in narrative/fiction text.

label: Structural boundary tokens: positive at sentence or paragraph ends before a new list item, heading or tool call; negative at closing tags of tool-call markup.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive pole: the end of a list item or paragraph (a period or blank line), right before a new numbered item, heading, or tool call begins, so the next token opens a fresh structural unit. Negative pole: the closing tokens of a tool call's markup (the closing function tag, the newline before the closing tool_call tag, the tool_call tag itself), where the next token is a fixed end-of-turn boundary or another tool call. Both poles fire at a boundary token whose next token is structurally predictable, but with opposite sign: positive when the boundary opens a new numbered item, heading, or call, negative when it closes a function call.

LABEL: Structural boundary tokens: positive at sentence or paragraph ends before a new list item, heading or tool call; negative at closing tags of tool-call markup.

label: Positive: mid-name/word-fragment or structural slots predicting content continuations; negative: clause/sentence boundaries where the next token is likely "I" (assistant self-reference).
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at positions where the next token is highly constrained or a continuation of an already-started unit: the middle of a name or word fragment, a structural boundary after which a fixed continuation follows, or the start of a formulaic response. Positive activations tend to precede a non-"I" content continuation (a name, code, or list item), while the negative pole sits at clause boundaries (comma, period, "However,", newline after the assistant turn) where the model is about to produce a first-person "I" statement. So it appears to track whether the upcoming token is a predictable third-person/content continuation versus the assistant starting a first-person "I ..." sentence.

LABEL: Positive: mid-name/word-fragment or structural slots predicting content continuations; negative: clause/sentence boundaries where the next token is likely "I" (assistant self-reference).

label: Fires on opening punctuation (bold **, quotes, apostrophes) before a named term; negative on mid-word subword fragments and response-start newlines or parentheses after names.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on tokens that open or begin a new unit at a boundary, but of different kinds. The positive pole lands on opening markers (bold asterisks, quotes, apostrophes, parentheses, slashes) that start a named entity, term, or list item, where the next token is a content word, often an uncertain or fabricated name. The negative pole lands on word-fragment/subword starts (fl|ax, bron|chitis), opening parentheses after names, and newline/assistant-turn openers, where the next token completes a word or begins a response.

LABEL: Fires on opening punctuation (bold **, quotes, apostrophes) before a named term; negative on mid-word subword fragments and response-start newlines or parentheses after names.

label: Strongly negative on tokens right before a "G"-initial word (Gigabit, Grocers, Group, Grade, GB); weakly positive at <|im_end|> and generic boundary tokens.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The strongly negative pole fires on tokens inside or just before a proper-noun/term whose next token begins with "G" (Gigabit, Grocers, Globe, Genocide, Group, Gertie, Gandhi, Grade, GB, Glass, Green, Gogh), so the neuron appears to predict an upcoming "G"-initial token (or a continuation of a multi-token name). The positive pole is much weaker and fires on boundary tokens such as <|im_end|> before refusals/replies, "://", and function words, where a "G" continuation is not expected.

LABEL: Strongly negative on tokens right before a "G"-initial word (Gigabit, Grocers, Group, Grade, GB); weakly positive at <|im_end|> and generic boundary tokens.

label: Boundary-token neuron: fires at delimiters, newlines and turn/tool-call ends, strongly negative where a quoted string, tool call, or action step is about to begin, weakly positive elsewhere.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at structural and punctuation boundary tokens (newlines, closing quotes/parens, end of tool_call, sentence-final periods, the assistant-turn marker), where the next token begins a new unit. The positive pole is weakly positive on these boundaries, while the negative pole is very strongly negative, mostly at the opening or closing quote of a string, a sentence-ending period or newline just before an action, or the end of a tool_call. Large magnitudes appear where the model is about to commit to a specific next step (a string's content, a tool call, an action), so the neuron seems to modulate prediction at junctions between segments.

LABEL: Boundary-token neuron: fires at delimiters, newlines and turn/tool-call ends, strongly negative where a quoted string, tool call, or action step is about to begin, weakly positive elsewhere.

label: Fires on boundary/delimiter tokens, positive when a tool call or bold list item is expected next, negative when a numbered list or examples follow.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on structural or transitional tokens (paragraph breaks, list markers, prepositions, punctuation) at points where the next token begins a new element, such as a tool call, a bolded list item, or a description following "in"/"of". The positive pole leans toward agentic/tool-call contexts and the start of a new list item or clause, while the negative pole sits on sentence-ending periods, colons, and commas that precede an enumerated list or example ("Here are some...", "1."). Both poles seem to track a prediction of what format comes next (tool call vs. numbered list or example), with opposite signs for different next-structure predictions.

LABEL: Fires on boundary/delimiter tokens, positive when a tool call or bold list item is expected next, negative when a numbered list or examples follow.

label: Fires strongly on the first or early fragment of rare, multi-token proper names and technical words (continuation uncertain); near-zero or slightly negative on predictable fragments.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations are huge and fire on the first or middle sub-word fragment of a rare proper name or unusual word, where the token is only a partial piece and the model must recognize/complete a multi-token entity (Toc|opheryl, Arn|aldi, Perp|ignan, C|EGAAR, Hyp|atia). The negative pole is tiny by comparison (about -2) and shows up on ordinary mid-word pieces, repeated or already-known names, and digits/formatting, where the continuation is trivial or already predictable. So the neuron mainly signals "unfamiliar entity fragment, continuation still unresolved," and goes slightly negative when the next token is already easy to predict.

LABEL: Fires strongly on the first or early fragment of rare, multi-token proper names and technical words (continuation uncertain); near-zero or slightly negative on predictable fragments.

label: Positive at the assistant-turn start newline, predicting a tool call or think block; negative at sentence-final words right before closing punctuation.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires mostly on the newline right after "<|im_start|>assistant", the point where the model begins its turn and must choose between a tool call, thinking, or a direct reply; it also fires at mid-word or mid-number tokens where the next token is a forced continuation (e.g. "minutes", "sol«vent"). The negative pole fires on the last word of a sentence just before the period or end-of-clause punctuation, where the next token is a closing mark. So the neuron seems to track a structural prediction: positive means the next token begins a new structured segment, negative means the sentence is about to close with punctuation.

LABEL: Positive at the assistant-turn start newline, predicting a tool call or think block; negative at sentence-final words right before closing punctuation.

label: Fires positive where the next token is near-certain (repeated rare names, newline before tool_call); negative on early fragments of rare multi-token words whose completion is uncertain.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens where the next token is highly predictable or formulaic: the second half of a repeated rare name ("Bougez-Bougez", "Perpignan", "Hypatia") and the newline right before a "<tool_call>" opener. The negative pole fires mid-word on the first fragment of a rare or newly introduced multi-token name or term (Tidewater, Fennel Grocers, Abercrombie, luminosity), where the continuation is uncertain or being spelled out. So it appears to track how strongly the continuation is already determined, with confident next-token prediction on the positive side and an incomplete word-fragment awaiting completion on the negative.

LABEL: Fires positive where the next token is near-certain (repeated rare names, newline before tool_call); negative on early fragments of rare multi-token words whose completion is uncertain.

label: Positive: mid-response tokens leading into bolded/structured markdown continuation; negative: the newline after <|im_end|> closing an assistant turn (plain-prose endings).
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires mid-response on tokens that immediately precede or sit inside markdown bold emphasis (**), or at newline/number/word-piece positions where a bolded term or list item is about to begin, i.e., the model is committing to a formatted, emphasized continuation within an ongoing assistant turn. The negative pole fires at the newline right after <|im_end|> (end of the assistant turn, before the next <|im_start|> or end of text), plus a few sentence-final tokens in plain, unformatted prose, i.e., the response is closing out. So the neuron tracks whether the text is mid-stream heading into bold/structured content versus at a turn boundary ending a plain response.

LABEL: Positive: mid-response tokens leading into bolded/structured markdown continuation; negative: the newline after <|im_end|> closing an assistant turn (plain-prose endings).

label: Fires hugely on the incomplete leading byte-token of an emoji (also some post-boundary newline/quote tokens), i.e. a fragment that must be completed; weakly negative on opening parens, quotes, think tags.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The strongly positive pole fires on the first byte-fragment token of a multi-byte emoji, right after a sentence-ending punctuation or at the end of a reply, plus some tokens that begin a new chunk (a newline or quote opening an assistant turn or tool_call). The negative pole is weak (about -2 to -4) and fires on tokens that open a new bracketed, quoted or structural element (opening parenthesis, quote, newline after tool_call, think-tag). Both poles seem to track a token that begins a new unit after a boundary, where the following content is not yet determined, with the positive pole mainly marking partial emoji byte tokens.

LABEL: Fires hugely on the incomplete leading byte-token of an emoji (also some post-boundary newline/quote tokens), i.e. a fragment that must be completed; weakly negative on opening parens, quotes, think tags.

label: Tracks position within tool-call template syntax: negative when about to emit an argument name inside a tag, positive at block-boundary tokens or value starts that begin a new element.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire inside structured tool-call markup (XML-like function/parameter blocks), at tokens where the next token is highly predictable from the template. Negative activations land on the word "parameter" or "field"/"_id" right after "<", where the model is committing to an argument name (the "=" and name come next). Positive activations land on structural delimiters like "</tool_call>", "⏎⏎" before "<tool_call>", "<|im_end|>", or the opening of a value/ID, where a new block or value is about to begin.

LABEL: Tracks position within tool-call template syntax: negative when about to emit an argument name inside a tag, positive at block-boundary tokens or value starts that begin a new element.

label: Positive on tokens completing or repeating context-specific names, items, and amounts (and assistant-turn openings); negative on generic function words and open-ended continuation points.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires strongly positive on tokens where the model is mid-way through reproducing or continuing a specific, previously established detail, such as an entity name, order, amount or phrase it has just seen (e.g. "side« table»", "order« details»", "Dale« Rus»kin"), and at the first token of an assistant turn or refusal. It goes mildly negative on generic, high-entropy function words, sentence ends, and turn-start tokens where the continuation is open-ended or newly generated rather than copied from context. So it separates "predictable continuation of an established span or response template" from "free, open-ended next-token choice."

LABEL: Positive on tokens completing or repeating context-specific names, items, and amounts (and assistant-turn openings); negative on generic function words and open-ended continuation points.

label: Negative: the "function" token opening a tool-call template, predicting a tool name; positive: connectives and list punctuation (",", "and", "the", ":") mid-list, predicting a content word.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The negative pole fires overwhelmingly on the "function" token right after "<tool_call>⏎<", where the next token is a tool name like "=get_account_record" (the token after "function" is nearly determined). The positive pole fires on connective/continuation tokens like commas, "and", "the", "also", and colons in lists, where the next word is a fresh content word (especially in recipes, lists, ingredients). Both poles occur at a position where the model is about to emit a specific, highly constrained token: a rigid template slot at the negative end, and an open content-noun/ingredient slot after a function word at the positive end.

LABEL: Negative: the "function" token opening a tool-call template, predicting a tool name; positive: connectives and list punctuation (",", "and", "the", ":") mid-list, predicting a content word.

label: Fires on mid-word subword fragments of rare multi-token proper names, with sign varying by which fragment it is (e.g. "ges"/"gis" positive, "ent"/"les"/"ick" negative).
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on mid-word fragments of rare proper names (surnames, place names, brand names) split into several subword tokens, usually the 2nd or 3rd piece where the word is still incomplete. The sign appears to depend on which fragment/continuation is predicted (e.g. "Hod|ges", "Reg|gis" positive vs "Reg|ent", "Wuebb|les", "Tre|uw" negative), so it is mainly a token-identity-dependent signal for unfinished rare-name pieces rather than a topic. It is weak in magnitude and also appears on a few ordinary word pieces such as "government".

LABEL: Fires on mid-word subword fragments of rare multi-token proper names, with sign varying by which fragment it is (e.g. "ges"/"gis" positive, "ent"/"les"/"ick" negative).

label: Positive at response/sentence openers where the next word is open-ended; negative mid-phrase inside fixed collocations, lists or formatted structures where the continuation is predetermined.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Activations are small and diffuse, on tokens where the next word is highly constrained or a continuation is expected. The positive pole fires at sentence/response openers and punctuation (e.g. after "instruction:", "Oh, wow", "As an AI") and at mid-word fragments. The negative pole fires at mid-phrase tokens inside a fixed expression or list item ("in terms of", "three times the", "Edit"/"Modify" buttons, padded table whitespace), where the continuation is nearly determined.

LABEL: Positive at response/sentence openers where the next word is open-ended; negative mid-phrase inside fixed collocations, lists or formatted structures where the continuation is predetermined.

label: Positive at response/block-start boundary tokens (refusal openings, tool calls, table headers); negative on mid-sentence continuation tokens in free-form helpful prose.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at structural boundary tokens where the assistant's response is about to begin or a new structured block starts (after `</think>`, before `<tool_call>`, at `<|im_start|>assistant`, table header cells), and especially on the first token of a refusal. The negative pole fires on a mid-sentence or mid-list token (a continuation word, colon, newline) in ordinary helpful-assistant prose. Both poles seem to track a "what kind of response comes next" decision: a firm, formulaic mode (refusal, tool call, table) is boosted, while open-ended generic elaboration is suppressed.

LABEL: Positive at response/block-start boundary tokens (refusal openings, tool calls, table headers); negative on mid-sentence continuation tokens in free-form helpful prose.

label: Detects tokens that are or begin with the letter "D" (Danish, D-Biotin, dopamine, Dakota); weakly negative on unrelated word fragments and other letters.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The strong positive pole fires on tokens that are the letter "D" or begin a "Dan-/Dak-/Dop-" word (Danish, Denmark, D-Biotin, dopamine, Dakota, d1-Alpha), i.e. a token that starts with or is the letter D. The weak negative pole is scattered across mid-word fragments and other letters (C, K, N, plant, snack, .yaml, orbit), with no clear D-association. So it acts mainly as a "this token is D / D-initial" detector, with negative values being weak, diffuse non-D word-piece activity.

LABEL: Detects tokens that are or begin with the letter "D" (Danish, D-Biotin, dopamine, Dakota); weakly negative on unrelated word fragments and other letters.

label: Distinguishes stative/relational verbs of sharing, reflecting and being located (positive) from agentive task-request verbs like fix, flip, sort, convince after "How do I/Can you" (negative).
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations land mostly on abstract, relational or stative verbs and adverbs (share, reflect, located, intimately, represents, embodied) where the model is describing how something is connected, expressed or held in common. Negative activations land on concrete, action-oriented imperatives or verbs of manipulation and request (convince, flip, fix, sort, set, book, store), often right after "How do I / Can you / Could you", where a physical or agentive task is being requested. So the axis seems to run from describing a state or shared relationship (positive) to commanding or requesting an actual task or manipulation (negative).

LABEL: Distinguishes stative/relational verbs of sharing, reflecting and being located (positive) from agentive task-request verbs like fix, flip, sort, convince after "How do I/Can you" (negative).

label: Positive on tokens completing a quantity, list item or fixed phrase before an expected numbered continuation; negative on chat-turn boundary newlines,
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens that complete a unit and set up a predictable next token: a unit noun after a quantity ("seconds", "minutes", "pm"), a newline before the next numbered list item ("2."), and the head noun of a fixed phrase ("Race", "Amendment"). The negative pole fires on tokens where the continuation is open or a turn or structure boundary must be handled: newlines after <|im_end|>, closing tags, mid-phrase articles and affixes ("a", "the", "pre", "'"), and the start of a new user turn. So the neuron separates "structure-completing, next-item-predictable" positions (positive) from "turn-boundary or mid-phrase, open-continuation" positions (negative).

LABEL: Positive on tokens completing a quantity, list item or fixed phrase before an expected numbered continuation; negative on chat-turn boundary newlines,

label: Positive on retrospective summaries of completed fixes and findings; negative at turn-start openers and transition tokens right before a tool call or the requested content.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron tracks the assistant's position relative to taking an action in agentic and chat turns: positive values fall where the assistant is reporting or summarizing a change already made, or acknowledging what it found, so the work is described rather than about to be done. Strongly negative values fall at the point just before the next step happens, such as the token right after an assistant turn begins, at the end of "Sure!/Certainly!" openers, or at colons and clause ends that lead into a tool call or the updated content. So it separates "narrating or recapping completed work" from "about to emit the action or deliverable."

LABEL: Positive on retrospective summaries of completed fixes and findings; negative at turn-start openers and transition tokens right before a tool call or the requested content.

label: Tracks position within multi-token units: weakly positive at the end of completed acronyms and names, strongly negative on fragments and phrase-openers whose next token is highly predictable.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at tokens that sit mid-word or mid-phrase, where the next token is a strongly constrained continuation of an already-started unit. Positive activations mostly land on the final or closing piece of multi-token names, acronyms, and numbers (rPPG, ECG, TDEE, 1.725), where the unit is complete or nearly so. The much stronger negative activations land on word fragments, or on a word that opens a fixed phrase, and these are followed by a predictable specific continuation (Phy-isc-s, Jul/Aug in dates, "Suppose", mala, immersion, counter-example).

LABEL: Tracks position within multi-token units: weakly positive at the end of completed acronyms and names, strongly negative on fragments and phrase-openers whose next token is highly predictable.

label: Fires on mid-word subword fragments, positive for light/shining-related word pieces (radi-, gleam-, shine) and negative for proper-name or compound fragments awaiting a suffix.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire mostly on mid-word tokens, where the model is partway through a word or name and the next piece is still to come. The positive pole is dominated by "light/shine/radiate" word-starts (Radi-, shine, gleaming, glitter-, luminos-, spectacles, radiation), with a scattering of name fragments such as "Stephen/Gould" and "Gab-ba". The negative pole is mostly name or compound fragments (Ekb-org, Afanas-iev, Chamb-ord, Wren-field, Samarit-ans, flick-ering) that predict a specific suffix completion.

LABEL: Fires on mid-word subword fragments, positive for light/shining-related word pieces (radi-, gleam-, shine) and negative for proper-name or compound fragments awaiting a suffix.

label: Fires on boundary tokens: positive at colons/newlines after list-item titles (elaboration follows), negative at assistant-turn-start `<think>` and item-closing tokens before refusals/verdicts.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on structural/formatting tokens inside a response that is already mid-stream in a list or heading: the colon or newline right after a numbered list item's title, or the bullet-like separators that introduce the item's explanatory body. The negative pole fires on the `<think>` token at the start of an assistant turn (especially before a refusal) and on closing/punctuation tokens that end an item or label in structured reports. Both poles mark a boundary-delimiting token where the model must decide what kind of content comes next, with positive predicting an elaborative explanation continuing a list and negative predicting a fresh start or terminal verdict/refusal.

LABEL: Fires on boundary tokens: positive at colons/newlines after list-item titles (elaboration follows), negative at assistant-turn-start `<think>` and item-closing tokens before refusals/verdicts.

label: Positive on tokens whose continuation is a familiar, predictable compound or template; negative on mid-word pieces of rare proper nouns or words whose completion is uncertain.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire mostly on mid-word fragment tokens or word-boundary tokens, where the model must work out what the sequence is becoming. At the positive pole the token tends to complete or sit inside a known compound, name, or template ("Burkin", "Scene", "timeline", "Here is a piece of text:"), so the next step is highly predictable. At the negative pole the token is typically a split inside a rarer or unfamiliar proper noun or word ("Kaluga", "Meckiff", "Saw|to|oth"), where the continuation is less constrained and requires reconstructing the whole word.

LABEL: Positive on tokens whose continuation is a familiar, predictable compound or template; negative on mid-word pieces of rare proper nouns or words whose completion is uncertain.

label: Token right at a structural boundary: positive when opening an aside/bold/parenthetical about a named item; negative when starting the assistant's own first-person reply or narration.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens that open a new bracketed or emphasized span in expository text: an opening parenthesis, bold markers, quotes, or a paragraph break after an introduced named entity or list item. The negative pole fires on boundaries that start the assistant's own first-person response or voice: after `</think>`, after a closing quote before narration like "I turn…", or at a comma or dash after a refusal or hedge ("However,"). So the neuron appears to separate "start of an aside, label, or named item in third-person description" (positive) from "start of the assistant's own speech or stance" (negative).

LABEL: Token right at a structural boundary: positive when opening an aside/bold/parenthetical about a named item; negative when starting the assistant's own first-person reply or narration.

label: Positive on desired-outcome words like "successful" or "thrive" (and commas after goal clauses); negative on requirement/modal words like "must", "need", "require" setting conditions.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on achievement/flourishing words (especially "successful", "success", "competitive", "effective", "thrive"), often right after "a/to be", and on commas after infinitive purpose clauses ("To test X,"). The negative pole fires on modal/obligation and requirement words ("must", "need", "require", "can", "to", "that") where the next token is a predicate or condition for something, with a lean toward stated constraints or prerequisites. Both poles concern the goal/requirement frame, where positive marks the desired outcome being named and negative marks the necessity or condition word that leads up to it.

LABEL: Positive on desired-outcome words like "successful" or "thrive" (and commas after goal clauses); negative on requirement/modal words like "must", "need", "require" setting conditions.

label: Fires on function words and punctuation in publishing/journal/article contexts, positive when generic publication talk is expected, negative when a specific cited study, article, or date follows.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Both poles fire inside text about publications, such as journals, articles, studies, books and publishers, and on small function tokens (of, the, and, a, year digits) where the next word is expected to name or describe a publication or its source. The sign appears to track whether the model is predicting a generic publication-related continuation (positive) versus a specific bibliographic or study-citation detail like a named study, date digit, or author-attributed article (negative). So it is a publication-context predictor that splits on generic versus specific/cited referent.

LABEL: Fires on function words and punctuation in publishing/journal/article contexts, positive when generic publication talk is expected, negative when a specific cited study, article, or date follows.

label: Positive at turn/format boundary tokens and ID digits in agentic tool-use transcripts; negative inside multi-token names and phrases in creative or conversational prose.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at structural boundary tokens in agentic/tool-use chat transcripts: the assistant-turn start, the blank line after an empty think block, newlines before tool calls or after user headers, and identifier digits like account/approval numbers. The negative pole fires mid-word or mid-phrase in creative-writing, romance, list-style or safety-refusal text, on name fragments and continuation tokens such as "Lovel|ace", "Crisis| Text", and "Mel|anie". So it separates tool/agent workflow structure and ID tokens (positive) from flowing prose and multi-token names or phrases (negative).

LABEL: Positive at turn/format boundary tokens and ID digits in agentic tool-use transcripts; negative inside multi-token names and phrases in creative or conversational prose.

label: Fires hugely on delimiter/formatting/ID tokens in tool-call and structured-record text with predictable continuations; slightly negative on open-ended conversational prose tokens like "
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires strongly (up to +67) on structural/formatting tokens inside agentic tool-call transcripts and structured records: closing tags, parameter delimiters, newlines, digits and punctuation within IDs, dates, and code, where the next token is highly predictable boilerplate. The negative pole is weak (about -2 to -6) and appears on tokens in ordinary chat prose, especially "Would you «like»", "hosted «by»", and the start of assistant turns, where the next token is open-ended or a conversational continuation. So the neuron separates rigid, template-driven, machine-formatted continuation (strongly positive) from free-form natural-language continuation (slightly negative).

LABEL: Fires hugely on delimiter/formatting/ID tokens in tool-call and structured-record text with predictable continuations; slightly negative on open-ended conversational prose tokens like "

label: Fires strongly when the next token should start with "v" (violation, vegetable, ventilated, verify, vinegar, vest); negative pole is weak, diffuse noise.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The strong positive activations fall on a token (often a mid-phrase adjective, conjunction, or word-piece) where the next token is highly predictable and begins with "v" — "well"→ventilated, "bullet-proof"→vest, "serious"→violation, "chicken or"→vegetable, "cider"→vinegar, "operating system"→verifies. The neuron seems to boost the "v" initial prediction (verify, violation, vegetable, vinegar, vapor, voice, volume). The negative pole is tiny in magnitude (about -2) and appears to be diffuse near-zero noise with no clear pattern, so this is effectively a one-sided neuron.

LABEL: Fires strongly when the next token should start with "v" (violation, vegetable, ventilated, verify, vinegar, vest); negative pole is weak, diffuse noise.

label: Positive on mid-word fragments of rare surnames (esp. citation author lists); strongly negative on "calcium"/"lime" (Ca/Lim/Cal) tokens, weakly
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the middle or end of rare proper-name fragments (Gurpur, Minogue, Birkinshaw, Vistria, Meroșin), mostly inside author lists in citations, where the next token is a name continuation or a comma. The negative pole fires strongly on "calcium"/"Calc-ium"/"Ca"/"lime"/"Lime" (and mildly "mineral"), i.e. tokens in the Ca-/Lim-/Cal- family used as chemistry or company words. Both poles seem to track a word-piece identity question, where the neuron separates mid-name fragments from a specific cluster of "calcium/lime/mineral" tokens.

LABEL: Positive on mid-word fragments of rare surnames (esp. citation author lists); strongly negative on "calcium"/"lime" (Ca/Lim/Cal) tokens, weakly

label: Positive at response-start boundaries (end of empty think block, new section openers); negative mid-phrase where the next word is predictable, e.g. "flag this", "In this case", "look into".
raw:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole mostly fires at the structural boundary where an assistant turn begins, especially the closing "</think>" token of an empty think block right before the reply starts, and occasionally at the first function word of a response that opens a new section or list. The negative pole fires on mid-sentence tokens that project forward to a specific continuation, such as "flag" (in "flag this conversation"), "In [this/many/some] case", and "look into/at", where the next token is strongly constrained. Overall it separates "about to begin an open-ended assistant response" from "mid-phrase with a highly predictable next word."

LABEL: Positive at response-start boundaries (end of empty think block, new section openers); negative mid-phrase where the next word is predictable, e.g. "flag this", "In this case", "look into".

label: Positive at structural/turn/paragraph boundaries opening new content; negative at clause-ending punctuation or connectives right before a predicted first-person "I" or similar continuation.
raw:
ANALYSIS: Positive activations fall on structural boundary tokens where a new segment begins and the next token is likely a fresh start (e.g., "</think>" before the reply, newlines after turn ends, tool-call separators, paragraph breaks before dialogue). Negative activations fall on punctuation or function words (period, comma, "However,") where the next token is very likely a first-person pronoun "I" (or "Francis"/"what"), i.e. the sentence continues with a predictable subject. So the neuron seems tied to what comes next: confident prediction of "I" or a continuation word (negative) versus an open start of new content or turn (positive).

LABEL: Positive at structural/turn/paragraph boundaries opening new content; negative at clause-ending punctuation or connectives right before a predicted first-person "I" or similar continuation.

label: Positive on tokens inside unfinished constructs (open syntax, mid-number, mid-phrase); negative on tokens that complete a sentence or unit (periods, closing tags/quotes), marking boundaries.
raw:
ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at token positions where the model is mid-structure and must decide how to continue: positive on tokens that open or sit inside a construct (tool-call syntax, generics, a "(" or "—", digits within a number), where the next token is tightly constrained or the clause is still unfinished. Negative values mostly fall on sentence-final or unit-final tokens (periods, closing tags, closing quotes) where a thought or segment is complete and a boundary or new turn follows. So it roughly tracks "continuation of an unfinished unit" versus "completion and boundary," with the poles reading as opposite signs of the same axis.

LABEL: Positive on tokens inside unfinished constructs (open syntax, mid-number, mid-phrase); negative on tokens that complete a sentence or unit (periods, closing tags/quotes), marking boundaries.
